screens.title: VM Program Flow: Labels, Goto, If-Goto
screens.narratorSegment: Program flow is the backbone of any program: it decides which instructions run and when. In this chapter you'll learn the VM's three flow primitives — label, goto, and if-goto — and how they map to Hack assembly labels and jumps. We'll see how labels mark positions, how goto performs unconditional jumps, and how if-goto pops a condition and jumps only when that value is true. You'll also learn an important practical detail: VM labels are local to a function, but the assembler uses a global namespace, so the translator must create unique names by prefixing labels with the function name. Concrete examples will show how to implement if-then, if-then-else, while and for loops using only these commands. Finally, you'll be guided through simple translation patterns and a short testing activity that helps you verify your VM translator by running the generated assembly in the simulator. By the end, you should be able to translate VM flow commands to assembly, reason about the control-flow patterns they create, and avoid common mistakes such as label collisions or incorrect popping before conditional jumps. Which control-flow shape will you try translating first?

Third, you'll reason about label scope: VM labels are function-local, but assembly labels are global, so you'll practice name mangling by prefixing labels with the function name to avoid collisions. screens.title: The three VM flow commands
screens.narratorSegment: Start by internalizing the semantics of the three VM commands. A label declares a named position in VM code; it does not change the stack or registers, it simply marks the current instruction so other flow commands can jump to it. Goto is an unconditional transfer of control: when executed, subsequent instructions continue at the target label. If-goto is the conditional variant. It inspects the top-of-stack value, pops it, and if that value is non-zero it jumps to the named label; otherwise execution proceeds to the next instruction. A concrete example: to branch only when a comparison is true, you push operands, execute a comparison command like gt, then use if-goto with the label of the true branch. A common misconception is thinking if-goto leaves the condition on the stack; it does not — it must pop so the condition value doesn't pollute later computations. Another confusion arises about label placement: labels are declarations positioned where you want control to resume. Remember these three operations — mark, jump, conditional jump — are enough to express all control flow patterns. To check your understanding, imagine implementing a small if-then by combining one comparison, one if-goto, and two labels. What will be popped and what will remain on the stack at the end?

content.html:
Core Concept
The three VM flow commands
Precise semantics and a short example to ground meaning.
Label
Declares a position in code to target with jumps; no stack effect.
Goto
Unconditional transfer: subsequent execution continues at the label.
If-Goto
Pops the top-of-stack; if non-zero, it jumps to the label; otherwise it falls through.
Concrete example
push local 0    // x
push local 1    // y
gt              // x > y?
if-goto IF_TRUE
// else block
push local 1
push local 0
sub
pop local 1
goto IF_END
label IF_TRUE
// if block
push local 0
push local 1
sub
pop local 0
label IF_END
Misconception
If-goto does not keep the condition on the stack; it consumes it. Forgetting this leads to extra values that break later stack-based ops.
Key Takeaway

These three simple commands — mark, unconditional jump, conditional pop-and-jump — compose to produce all higher-level branching and loops.

screens.title: Translating label to assembly
screens.narratorSegment: Translating a VM label is the simplest mapping: a label declaration in VM corresponds to an assembler label in Hack. In VM you write label LOOP to mark a position. The translator should output an assembly label declaration that the Hack assembler understands: a parenthesized symbol like (LOOP). But there's an important practical rule: VM labels are scoped to their function. When the translator flattens code into assembly it must guarantee uniqueness across the whole program, otherwise two functions that use the same VM label name will collide during assembly. The usual strategy is to prefix the VM label with the current function name and a separator, for example Main. main$LOOP. This keeps labels readable and unique. A concrete translation step is: on encountering label X inside function F, emit (F$X) into the assembly. One common mistake is emitting the VM label verbatim without prefixing; that will work only if the label name is globally unique by chance. Another is generating prefixes inconsistently, which also causes mismatches when goto targets are emitted. To validate your implementation, translate a small program with the same label used in two functions and ensure the assembler accepts the output. What naming scheme will you choose for your translator?

keyIdea.title: Label declaration rule
keyIdea.text: Emit (FunctionName$LabelName) so assembly symbols are globally unique while remaining traceable to the VM code.

content.html:
Definition → Assembly
Translating VM label
Make label declarations the assembler understands while preserving uniqueness.
Pattern
VM: label LOOP
Assembly: (FunctionName$LOOP)
Example: label LOOP inside Main.main becomes (Main.main$LOOP) so goto Main.main$LOOP and if-goto Main.main$LOOP match the symbol.
Validation
Translate two functions that both declare label LOOP. The assembler should accept the output because names are distinct after prefixing.
Common mistakes
  • Emitting the VM label verbatim so duplicate names collide at assembly time.
  • Using inconsistent separators so goto targets don't match label declarations.
  • Forgetting to update current-function context while translating nested code fragments.
Key Takeaway

Always mangle VM labels with the current function name when emitting assembly declarations to avoid global name collisions.

screens.title: Translating goto
screens.narratorSegment: The VM goto command requests an unconditional transfer of control to a named label. In assembly, this is implemented by referencing the label symbol and issuing an unconditional jump instruction. For Hack assembly, the pattern is to reference the label with @Label and then issue 0;JMP to force control transfer. If the VM label belongs to a function, ensure the same prefixing/mangling is applied to the target symbol so the @target matches a declared (prefixed) label. A translator must therefore emit two lines: one that loads the label address and one that performs the unconditional jump. A concrete example: translating goto LOOP inside function F yields @F$LOOP followed by 0;JMP in the assembly output. Misunderstandings arise when users try to use arithmetic conditions for unconditional jumps or when they emit labels without consistent prefixes. To test your code, create a short VM program with a goto that jumps to a label beyond several instructions and step the generated assembly in the simulator. Does control resume at the expected instruction after the jump? If not, check the emitted symbol names for consistency.

keyIdea.title: Goto → @Label + 0;JMP
keyIdea.text: Emit @Function$Label followed by 0;JMP so control unconditionally transfers to the target assembly label.

content.html:
Definition → Assembly
Translating goto
Unconditional transfer is mapped to a direct assembly jump.
// VM: goto LOOP
// Assembly (inside function F):
@F$LOOP
0;JMP
Because 0;JMP does not examine registers or the stack, it is the simplest way to force the program counter to a new label. Ensure symbol prefixing is applied to all goto targets so the @ instruction refers to the same global symbol declared by label emissions.
Test scenario
Translate a VM sequence that uses goto to skip a block. Step the assembly and observe that program counter jumps to the label location and resumes subsequent instructions from there.
Common mistake

Using a conditional jump by mistake or forgetting to prefix label symbols leads to unexpected fall-through behavior or assembly errors.

screens.title: Translating if-goto
screens.narratorSegment: If-goto is the VM's conditional branching primitive. Its translation must remove the top value from the stack and jump when that value is non-zero. In assembly you implement this by decrementing the stack pointer, loading the popped value into D, and then jumping if D is not zero. For Hack assembly the typical emission looks like this sequence: reference SP, decrement it, set D to the value, reference the label, and then use D;JNE to jump when D!= 0. The important semantic detail is that the condition is consumed; this keeps subsequent operations from seeing the predicate leftover on the stack. A common error is to test the top-of-stack without popping it, which leaves the value on the stack and corrupts later stack-based calculations. To validate, translate a VM sequence that pushes a boolean-like value, calls if-goto, and then check the stack depth and simulator trace after the conditional. Below is the canonical assembly pattern for if-goto that you should emit from your translator. Translating if-goto means pop the top-of-stack into d and emit d;jne to conditionally jump when d != 0; ensure the pop removes the value from the stack.. In practical terms, pop condition and jump if true. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: If-goto pattern
keyIdea.text: Pop the top-of-stack into D and emit D;JNE to conditionally jump when D != 0; ensure the pop removes the value from the stack.

content.html:
Definition → Assembly
Translating if-goto
Pop and conditionally jump when the value is non-zero.
@SP
AM=M-1
D=M      // D = top value (popped)
@FunctionName$LABEL
D;JNE    // Jump if D != 0
This sequence both updates SP and ensures the popped value is used as the branch condition. A translator emits the function-prefixed label name in the final two lines so the jump and the label declaration match globally.
Example scenario
Use if-goto after a comparison op like gt. The comparison leaves 0 or 1 on the stack; if-goto will pop that result and branch only when the comparison was true.
Pitfall

Not popping before testing duplicates the condition and changes stack positions for following instructions. Always consume the predicate with if-goto.

screens.title: Building an if-then structure
screens.narratorSegment: An if-then in VM is constructed by evaluating a condition, using if-goto to jump to the then-branch when true, and otherwise falling through to the next instructions. The translator emits labels and jump sequences to implement this shape. The common pattern is: evaluate condition, if-goto THEN, then-body (or else fallthrough), label THEN. A concrete VM example is: push local 0; push local 1; gt; if-goto IF_TRUE; // else-block... goto IF_END; label IF_TRUE; // if-block... label IF_END. Translating this to assembly uses the if-goto pattern that pops the comparison result then jumps, and goto to skip the else block when necessary. A misconception students often have is thinking an immediate fallthrough after if-goto executes the else-block automatically; in reality you must explicitly jump over the else-block when the condition was true. When you translate, ensure both labels are prefixed with the function name so the assembler sees unique symbols. For practice, translate the example and step through the assembled code to see how the stack values change and where the program counter moves on true and false outcomes. Building an if-then structure means use a conditional if-goto to enter the then branch and a goto to skip the else part. always declare matching labels and mangle names by function.. In practical terms, pattern and vm code example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
Building an if-then
Translate the VM pattern and observe how jumps control flow.
VM pattern
push local 0
push local 1
gt
if-goto IF_TRUE
// else block
... 
goto IF_END
label IF_TRUE
// if block
...
label IF_END
Step 1: Evaluate condition and leave 0/1 on stack.
Step 2: if-goto consumes the result and branches if true.
Step 3: Use goto to skip the else portion after executing the then block.
Step 4: Declare matching IF_END and IF_TRUE labels with function prefixing.
Concrete check
Translate and step through both branches in the simulator. Confirm that the then-block executes only when the comparison produced a non-zero value and that the stack is balanced afterwards.
Key Takeaway

An if-then is a short composition of evaluation, a conditional pop-and-jump, and label declarations — keep the stack discipline to avoid bugs.

screens.title: If-then-else pattern
screens.narratorSegment: The if-then-else structure uses both conditional and unconditional jumps so the translator must arrange labels and gotos carefully. The usual pattern is: evaluate the condition, if-goto ELSE, execute the then-block, goto END, label ELSE, execute else-block, label END. The conditional if-goto transfers control into the else label when the condition is true in some translation conventions; note the chapter example inverts the branch ordering for its logic. What matters is consistency between how the VM code arranges then and else blocks and the labels you emit. When translating, prefix both ELSE and END labels with the function name and emit corresponding assembly sequences: a pop-and-test followed by @Function$ELSE and D;JNE, then the then-block code, then @Function$END and 0;JMP, then declare (Function$ELSE) and emit else-block instructions, and finally (Function$END). A common source of bugs is swapped label names or forgetting the final goto that skips the else block; this causes both blocks to execute sequentially. To confirm correctness, step through the assembled program for both true and false conditions and verify that exactly one block executes each time. If-then-else pattern means use if-goto to choose between branches and a goto to skip the remaining branch; labels must be consistently prefixed to match declarations and targets.. In practical terms, two labels and two jumps implement else clauses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use if-goto to choose between branches and a goto to skip the remaining branch; labels must be consistently prefixed to match declarations and targets.

Process Flow
If-then-else pattern
Translate the structure so only one branch runs.
VM pattern (chapter example)
push local 0
push local 1
gt
if-goto IF_TRUE
// else block
push local 1
push local 0
sub
pop local 1
goto IF_END
label IF_TRUE
// if block
push local 0
push local 1
sub
pop local 0
label IF_END
When you translate, ensure the conditional jump consumes the comparison result and that the unconditional goto jumps past the else-block so the then-block does not fall through into else. Run both true and false cases in the simulator to validate behavior and stack cleanliness.
Pitfalls & checks
  • Swapping ELSE and END names by accident.
  • Omitting the goto that skips the else-block.
  • Not prefixing labels consistently across the translator output.
Key Takeaway

If-then-else requires clear control transfers: conditional branch into one label, an unconditional skip over the alternate, and consistent label declarations.

screens.title: While loop implementation
screens.narratorSegment: A while loop is implemented by placing a label at the loop start, evaluating the loop condition, using if-goto to jump to the end when the condition indicates termination, executing the loop body, and then using goto to return to the loop start. The chapter illustrates this pattern plainly: label WHILE_START; evaluate i < n with a comparison leaving 0 or 1 on the stack; if-goto WHILE_END; perform the body; update loop variables; goto WHILE_START; label WHILE_END. Translating this requires you to emit labels prefixed by the function name and to ensure the conditional check uses the pop-and-test pattern so the condition is removed from the stack. A practical check is to translate the sample while loop that sums and increments an index and then run the assembly with known initial values for i and n. Step through the simulator and count iterations to ensure the loop terminates when expected. screens.title: For loops and counters
screens.narratorSegment: A for loop is conceptually similar to a while loop; it adds an explicit initialization and an update step. The translator emits VM code that initializes loop variables, then enters a loop-start label, tests the loop condition, branches to the end when finished, executes the body, updates the counter, and jumps back to the start. The key translation decision is where to place the counter update: typically after the body and before the goto back to the loop start. The VM's label, goto and if-goto commands are sufficient: you emit label LOOP, push and compare the counter to the limit, if-goto LOOP_END, body operations, update the counter, goto LOOP, label LOOP_END. Because these pieces are identical in nature to the while pattern, the implementation overhead in your translator is modest. A practical example is initializing a counter to a constant, translating the compare and updates, and then verifying iteration counts in the simulator. Remember to mangle labels with the current function name so multiple for loops across functions cannot conflict. A common error is off-by-one updates; verify whether the loop condition should be strictly less than or less-or-equal and implement the comparison accordingly.

screens.title: Why three commands are enough
screens.narratorSegment: It's natural to ask why label, goto and if-goto suffice for all control structures. The reason is simple: every high-level control structure manipulates which instruction executes next, and that can be expressed with combinations of unconditional and conditional transfers of control. An if-then or if-then-else is implemented by a conditional branch and a skip-over goto. Loops are a repeated conditional test plus a goto back to the start. Even switch statements, breaks, and continues can be lowered to conditional tests and jumps. This minimality is important because it keeps the VM small and predictable while still expressive enough for a compiler to map constructs to VM sequences. A misconception is that lacking structured constructs makes programs unreadable; while assembly-level jumps are lower-level, the compiler (like Jack compiler) generates VM patterns that preserve structured behavior. For translator authors, the practical implication is that you only need correct implementations of these three primitives and label mangling to support any control-flow feature the compiler emits. How will you demonstrate this by compiling a small set of high-level constructs into VM flow commands? Why three commands are enough means conditional and unconditional jumps plus labels form a functionally complete set for expressing control flow; compilers lower structured constructs to these primitives.. In practical terms, expressing all control structures via jumps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Why three commands are enough
Unconditional and conditional transfers express all control-flow graphs.

Conditional jump to one label, and an unconditional jump to skip the alternate branch.

fullNarratorScript:
Program flow is the backbone of any program: it decides which instructions run and when. In this chapter you'll learn the VM's three flow primitives — label, goto, and if-goto — and how they map to Hack assembly labels and jumps. We'll see how labels mark positions, how goto performs unconditional jumps, and how if-goto pops a condition and jumps only when that value is true. You'll also learn an important practical detail: VM labels are local to a function, but the assembler uses a global namespace, so the translator must create unique names by prefixing labels with the function name. Concrete examples will show how to implement if-then, if-then-else, while and for loops using only these commands. Finally, you'll be guided through simple translation patterns and a short testing activity that helps you verify your VM translator by running the generated assembly in the simulator. By the end, you should be able to translate VM flow commands to assembly, reason about the control-flow patterns they create, and avoid common mistakes such as label collisions or incorrect popping before conditional jumps. Which control-flow shape will you try translating first?

These objectives focus your work on program flow in the VM. First, you'll implement label, goto, and if-goto in a VM translator so the translator emits correct Hack assembly. That task requires understanding both the VM semantics and the assembly instructions that perform jumps. Second, you'll learn to translate each VM command into assembly patterns that include label declarations, unconditional jumps, and conditional jumps that pop the top-of-stack and branch when true. Third, you'll reason about label scope: VM labels are function-local, but assembly labels are global, so you'll practice name mangling by prefixing labels with the function name to avoid collisions. Finally, you'll test control structures by translating simple if, if-else, while, and for examples and running them in the simulator. For each objective you'll get concrete examples and a small verification step so you know your translator produces correct behavior. Which objective will you tackle first — implementing the pop-and-jump for if-goto or adding function-prefixed label emission?

This second objectives slide focuses on practical verification. You will run small VM programs that exercise loops and branches, translate them to assembly, and trace execution in the C P U simulator. For example, a simple loop that decrements a counter can be translated to VM labels and jumps, and then you can count iterations by stepping the simulator. You'll also test conditional branching by pushing a condition, using if-goto and verifying the top-of-stack is popped during the jump. These steps teach you both the code-generation patterns and how to validate them in practice. We'll highlight common mistakes to watch for: forgetting to pop before a conditional jump, emitting duplicate labels without function prefixes, or emitting the wrong jump condition. By the end of the exercises you'll be able to diagnose failing traces and fix the translation logic. Which test will you run first — the loop that counts down or the if-then-else that chooses between two branches?

Start by internalizing the semantics of the three VM commands. A label declares a named position in VM code; it does not change the stack or registers, it simply marks the current instruction so other flow commands can jump to it. Goto is an unconditional transfer of control: when executed, subsequent instructions continue at the target label. If-goto is the conditional variant. It inspects the top-of-stack value, pops it, and if that value is non-zero it jumps to the named label; otherwise execution proceeds to the next instruction. A concrete example: to branch only when a comparison is true, you push operands, execute a comparison command like gt, then use if-goto with the label of the true branch. A common misconception is thinking if-goto leaves the condition on the stack; it does not — it must pop so the condition value doesn't pollute later computations. Another confusion arises about label placement: labels are declarations positioned where you want control to resume. Remember these three operations — mark, jump, conditional jump — are enough to express all control flow patterns. To check your understanding, imagine implementing a small if-then by combining one comparison, one if-goto, and two labels. What will be popped and what will remain on the stack at the end?

Translating a VM label is the simplest mapping: a label declaration in VM corresponds to an assembler label in Hack. In VM you write label LOOP to mark a position. The translator should output an assembly label declaration that the Hack assembler understands: a parenthesized symbol like (LOOP). But there's an important practical rule: VM labels are scoped to their function. When the translator flattens code into assembly it must guarantee uniqueness across the whole program, otherwise two functions that use the same VM label name will collide during assembly. The usual strategy is to prefix the VM label with the current function name and a separator, for example Main. main$LOOP. This keeps labels readable and unique. A concrete translation step is: on encountering label X inside function F, emit (F$X) into the assembly. One common mistake is emitting the VM label verbatim without prefixing; that will work only if the label name is globally unique by chance. Another is generating prefixes inconsistently, which also causes mismatches when goto targets are emitted. To validate your implementation, translate a small program with the same label used in two functions and ensure the assembler accepts the output. What naming scheme will you choose for your translator?

The VM goto command requests an unconditional transfer of control to a named label. In assembly, this is implemented by referencing the label symbol and issuing an unconditional jump instruction. For Hack assembly, the pattern is to reference the label with @Label and then issue 0;JMP to force control transfer. If the VM label belongs to a function, ensure the same prefixing/mangling is applied to the target symbol so the @target matches a declared (prefixed) label. A translator must therefore emit two lines: one that loads the label address and one that performs the unconditional jump. A concrete example: translating goto LOOP inside function F yields @F$LOOP followed by 0;JMP in the assembly output. Misunderstandings arise when users try to use arithmetic conditions for unconditional jumps or when they emit labels without consistent prefixes. To test your code, create a short VM program with a goto that jumps to a label beyond several instructions and step the generated assembly in the simulator. Does control resume at the expected instruction after the jump? If not, check the emitted symbol names for consistency.

If-goto is the VM's conditional branching primitive. Its translation must remove the top value from the stack and jump when that value is non-zero. In assembly you implement this by decrementing the stack pointer, loading the popped value into D, and then jumping if D is not zero. For Hack assembly the typical emission looks like this sequence: reference SP, decrement it, set D to the value, reference the label, and then use D;JNE to jump when D!= 0. The important semantic detail is that the condition is consumed; this keeps subsequent operations from seeing the predicate leftover on the stack. A common error is to test the top-of-stack without popping it, which leaves the value on the stack and corrupts later stack-based calculations. To validate, translate a VM sequence that pushes a boolean-like value, calls if-goto, and then check the stack depth and simulator trace after the conditional. Below is the canonical assembly pattern for if-goto that you should emit from your translator. Translating if-goto means pop the top-of-stack into d and emit d;jne to conditionally jump when d != 0; ensure the pop removes the value from the stack.. In practical terms, pop condition and jump if true. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An if-then in VM is constructed by evaluating a condition, using if-goto to jump to the then-branch when true, and otherwise falling through to the next instructions. The translator emits labels and jump sequences to implement this shape. The common pattern is: evaluate condition, if-goto THEN, then-body (or else fallthrough), label THEN. A concrete VM example is: push local 0; push local 1; gt; if-goto IF_TRUE; // else-block... goto IF_END; label IF_TRUE; // if-block... label IF_END. Translating this to assembly uses the if-goto pattern that pops the comparison result then jumps, and goto to skip the else block when necessary. A misconception students often have is thinking an immediate fallthrough after if-goto executes the else-block automatically; in reality you must explicitly jump over the else-block when the condition was true. When you translate, ensure both labels are prefixed with the function name so the assembler sees unique symbols. For practice, translate the example and step through the assembled code to see how the stack values change and where the program counter moves on true and false outcomes. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The if-then-else structure uses both conditional and unconditional jumps so the translator must arrange labels and gotos carefully. The usual pattern is: evaluate the condition, if-goto ELSE, execute the then-block, goto END, label ELSE, execute else-block, label END. The conditional if-goto transfers control into the else label when the condition is true in some translation conventions; note the chapter example inverts the branch ordering for its logic. What matters is consistency between how the VM code arranges then and else blocks and the labels you emit. When translating, prefix both ELSE and END labels with the function name and emit corresponding assembly sequences: a pop-and-test followed by @Function$ELSE and D;JNE, then the then-block code, then @Function$END and 0;JMP, then declare (Function$ELSE) and emit else-block instructions, and finally (Function$END). A common source of bugs is swapped label names or forgetting the final goto that skips the else block; this causes both blocks to execute sequentially. To confirm correctness, step through the assembled program for both true and false conditions and verify that exactly one block executes each time. If-then-else pattern means use if-goto to choose between branches and a goto to skip the remaining branch; labels must be consistently prefixed to match declarations and targets.. In practical terms, two labels and two jumps implement else clauses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A while loop is implemented by placing a label at the loop start, evaluating the loop condition, using if-goto to jump to the end when the condition indicates termination, executing the loop body, and then using goto to return to the loop start. The chapter illustrates this pattern plainly: label WHILE_START; evaluate i < n with a comparison leaving 0 or 1 on the stack; if-goto WHILE_END; perform the body; update loop variables; goto WHILE_START; label WHILE_END. A common mistake is testing for the loop condition using the wrong comparison sense or forgetting to update the loop variable, resulting in infinite loops or zero-iteration behavior. Remember: correct ordering of label, test, body, and goto is essential for intended loop behavior.

A for loop is conceptually similar to a while loop; it adds an explicit initialization and an update step. The translator emits VM code that initializes loop variables, then enters a loop-start label, tests the loop condition, branches to the end when finished, executes the body, updates the counter, and jumps back to the start. The key translation decision is where to place the counter update: typically after the body and before the goto back to the loop start. The VM's label, goto and if-goto commands are sufficient: you emit label LOOP, push and compare the counter to the limit, if-goto LOOP_END, body operations, update the counter, goto LOOP, label LOOP_END. A practical example is initializing a counter to a constant, translating the compare and updates, and then verifying iteration counts in the simulator. Let's summarize the essential points. First, the VM provides three flow primitives: label to mark positions, goto for unconditional jumps, and if-goto for conditional jumps that pop the condition. Second, when translating to Hack assembly, label declarations become parenthesized symbols, goto emits an @Label followed by 0;JMP, and if-goto requires popping the stack into a register and issuing a conditional jump like D;JNE. Third, VM labels are local to functions, but the assembler has a global symbol space, so translators must prefix labels with the function name to avoid collisions. Finally, with these three commands you can express if-then, if-then-else, while and for loops — the Jack compiler relies on these patterns to lower structured constructs.
